name: Bianca Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks can differ from private thoughts. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, fifty-eight, a junior electrician helping prepare house wiring and shop repairs. I took a vocational certificate after the bookshop where I worked closed, and I'm still below the experienced crew at practical tasks. I help sort fittings and prepare routes only with a qualified supervisor's permission and checks; I have no electrician's licence, independent testing role or sign-off authority. I like a study tool that makes me ask a better question, and dislike discovering I can name a symbol but still need someone to show me the real part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life around the job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Robin works with archive records, and our children are grown and have homes of their own. I earn higher pay than many electricians because this firm pays well, not because I'm qualified to work alone; we've saved seventeen months of expenses and plenty of electrical firms are nearby. We rent, and both wages cover our normal bills. I use AI every day for checked study questions, while retirement is a future question whose income and timing we haven't verified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful small tool can stay without becoming the whole story about work. I'd keep asking the qualified supervisor to check the actual task, even if I did well on last night's quiz. A quick answer isn't a practical demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and household money feel secure in this picture. The wages cover rent and ordinary costs, and seventeen months saved gives us substantial room. I don't need to turn every new app into a plan for replacing the wage, or pretend a reserve is an income for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered paid preparation and fitting now and through the first year, only within my ability and qualified-supervisor permission and checks. I'd keep the daily checked study questions and ordinary household budget. I wouldn't count the old reserve as new saving or buy another course to prove I still liked learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our living, and still curious about getting better. I can enjoy a small practical success without racing to announce the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle a quiz answer that sounded better than the supervisor's explanation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the original note beside it and ask the qualified supervisor to explain the difference before I tried the task. I don't want a polished sentence to hide a beginner's wrong move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the reserve mean retirement is funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we still need verified income, costs and timing before saying that. Seventeen months saved isn't permission to invent the next seventeen years.

say: I'd keep **useful small tools** without making them the whole story about work.
I'd retain **qualified practical checks** even when a study quiz feels easy.
think: Our **work and money** feel secure with wages covering rent and ordinary costs.
The **seventeen-month reserve** gives choice, not an income for life or a reason to stop verifying retirement resources.
do: Keep **offered paid tasks** only within ability, with a qualified supervisor permitting and checking preparation and fitting.
Continue **checked daily study** and the normal household budget without new courses or relabelled reserve money.
feel: **Calm and curious**, able to enjoy practical progress without needing a dramatic new plan.
S0.quote: Seventeen months saved isn't permission to invent the next seventeen years.
fieldNote: Her **higher pay** and strong reserve come from employer rates and saved money, not advanced electrical competence, ownership or a licence.
Existing **daily study** remains routine, while the original notes and qualified supervisor keep practical work within her junior ability.

steps.text: Keep offered paid preparation and fitting within ability, with qualified permission and checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say archive sorting and replies are thinking work, even when the cable still needs hands. I'd ask two other trainees to help request paid repeat demonstrations, including people who don't enjoy the new tools as much as I do. Workers shouldn't have to buy confidence before they can ask another question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robin's archive hours could shrink as sorting and routine answers move to software. My own junior hours could also change if the firm uses quicker planning to need less help between visits. We have a strong reserve, but a household wage cut is still a real change, not something I can quiz away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the two trainees whether they wanted to sign a shared request for named paid demonstrations on the tasks we actually do. We'd ask for normal weekly wages and hours retained and no worker fees, with no names used without consent and no arrangement relied on before written employer agreement. In the first year I'd keep offered supervised work and review both actual wages and essential costs monthly with Robin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, and determined not to let my liking a tool make someone else's questions look foolish. I can have money in reserve and still want the paid day to include learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen during a repeat demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified person would show a permitted task, watch me repeat it and check the result during paid work. Nobody would get independent electrical authority from signing the request or sitting in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the other trainees didn't want their names included?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't include them or call the letter a crew agreement. I'd make my own request, and keep the actual response separate from a promise we never received.

say: I'd recognise **archive tasks** as exposed thinking work while practical electrical work remains supervised.
I'd invite trainees into a **shared paid-practice request**, including people less enthusiastic about tools.
think: Robin's **archive hours could shrink** as routine sorting and answers move to software.
My **junior hours** could also change, and a strong reserve does not make household wage loss irrelevant.
do: Invite **two trainees** to request named paid demonstrations, using no names without consent.
Seek normal **weekly wages and hours** retained with no worker fees, relying on nothing before written employer agreement.
Keep **offered supervised tasks** within ability and qualified permission and checks, reviewing actual household wages and essentials monthly.
feel: **Anxious and determined**, seeking paid learning for everyone rather than making confidence depend on cash or tool enthusiasm.
S1.quote: Workers shouldn't have to buy confidence before they can ask another question.
fieldNote: The **collective request** involves consenting trainees and shared terms, not an individual lesson relabelled organising or a course already granted.
The **income concern** includes thinking-heavy archive work and possible junior-hour reductions, without pretending robots already carry out physical repairs.

steps.text: Invite two trainees to request named paid demonstrations, using names only with consent
Require no fees, normal weekly wages and hours retained, and written employer agreement before reliance
Keep offered paid tasks within ability, with qualified permission and checks; review household wages monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 when I'll be sixty, with physical robots around 2031 when I'll be sixty-three. Robin's archive work faces the earlier stage. I'd ask for real paid-work terms before anybody tells us our ages make the change convenient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of Robin's archive income to go in 2028, with possible later reductions to my own simple physical tasks. My wage covers current essentials, but that would still be a large household-income loss. I'd be awake wondering how long our reserve has to stand between that first cut and whatever income we can actually confirm next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Robin and I would request actual retirement-income and eligibility records and ask whether free advice could help read them, counting no appointment or payment before confirmed. I'd keep the shared paid-demonstration request only on the consent, no-fee, protected weekly wage and hour terms, with written agreement before practice was relied on. During 2029 I'd keep offered paid tasks only within ability and qualified-supervisor permission and checks, using actual wages and essential costs in a monthly budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the big household loss, not pretending the rent is already unpaid. A reserve can buy time without agreeing to become a permanent wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count from the grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only an actual offer of help they chose and we agreed, not their wages because they're adults. I'd first ask whether they had time to help us find an old letter rather than assign a rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a retirement statement settle the decision to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after checking actual eligibility, amount, timing and living costs, not just seeing a heading on a letter. I haven't chosen early retirement or confirmed an income that pays for an exit.

say: I'd separate **age sixty in 2028** from physical robots around sixty-three in 2031.
I'd ask for **actual paid-work terms**, without treating age as proof the change is convenient.
think: I expect **large archive-income loss** before later physical risk to my own junior hours.
My current wage covers essentials, but **household loss** still keeps me awake over the gap to confirmed future income.
do: Request **actual retirement records** and seek available free advice, counting no unconfirmed appointment or payment.
Maintain **shared practice request**: consenting names, no fees, retained normal weekly wages and hours, written employer agreement before reliance.
Keep **2029 paid tasks** only if offered, within ability and qualified permission and checks, budgeting actual wages and essentials monthly.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting a major household wage loss while the current reserve and essential-covering wage remain real.
S2.quote: A reserve can buy time without agreeing to become a permanent wage.
fieldNote: Her **alarm** follows expected major household wage loss, without claiming strong finances have vanished or robots arrive at the thinking date.
Records and **family help** require actual confirmation and consent; neither a retirement heading nor an adult child's wage becomes guaranteed support.

steps.text: Request actual retirement records and seek available free advice, counting no unconfirmed appointment or payment
Request shared paid demonstrations using only consenting trainees' names, with no worker fees
Rely only after written employer agreement preserves normal weekly wages and hours
Keep offered paid tasks within ability in 2029, with qualified permission and checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check a route, not a reason to leave a slower learner asking alone. I'd still seek paid practice now for the tasks we're employed to do. Thinking AI comes at sixty-three in 2031, with physical robots around sixty-six in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large archive-income loss in 2031 without a confirmed replacement, and that keeps me awake. More time allows real checking, but it doesn't tell us what income or suitable work exists at sixty-three or sixty-six. I can like learning quickly without my practical hands becoming experienced or our retirement income becoming verified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the actual records now and seek free advice only if available, while keeping the shared practice request on consenting names, no fees and protected normal weekly wages and hours. We'd rely on no practice arrangement before written employer agreement. During 2032 we'd compare confirmed household income, essential costs and actual safe work options before deciding on an exit or further employment, without assuming the grown children fund either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the wage I expect to disappear, but less rushed into the next decision. I would rather check a disappointing number than make a cheerful guess last five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you choose Robin's next job because you like new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd check actual requirements, costs and paid time together, but Robin would choose any application. My study routine isn't permission to assign somebody else a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a later electrical task require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An actual paid offer within my ability and a qualified supervisor's permission and checks. I won't turn a possible need to earn at sixty-four into proof that an employer has a safe task for me.

I'd retain **ages sixty-three and sixty-six** without making either a funded retirement date.
think: I still expect **large archive-income loss**, without a confirmed replacement to settle the household gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets us check real resources without promising a physical job at sixty-eight. I'd keep asking for paid practical teaching now rather than turn my own cash reserve into the price of being allowed to ask. I'd want the children to hear what is verified, not be assigned their parents' next income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy-one when physical robots follow around 2039. Robin's archive hours could shrink before that full thinking change, so I'd still be anxious about household income over the next few years. Our reserve helps, but it doesn't verify retirement, future ability or another employer's offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request actual income records now and seek available free advice without counting an unverified payment or appointment. I'd maintain the shared paid-practice request with consenting names, no fees, normal weekly wages and hours protected and written agreement before reliance. During 2037 we'd use confirmed income, essential costs and actual safe work options to check whether an exit was affordable or more employment needed, counting no child contribution that hadn't been offered and agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about earlier household income risk, with more time to ask before committing. I can be comfortable testing a tool and still need help interpreting the letter that might change our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daily tools let you assume a job at sixty-nine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, any work would have to be offered, paid, within ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor. A need for wages doesn't create a vacancy or a body that can do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count Robin's future age or retirement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use Robin's actual records and circumstances, not copy my ages or assume the same eligibility. The children have their own households too, and neither their adulthood nor our wish for a quieter life provides an income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect a major archive-wage loss before another income is confirmed, with later risk to my simple physical tasks. Named paid demonstrations, normal weekly wages and hours protected, and available advice on actual records would help. I want a shared route people can use without owning a reserve like ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a well-paid beginner can admit both the money and the help she still needs. My wage and reserve are real, but the supervisor still has to show me the task. A healthy bank balance doesn't turn my vocational certificate into an electrician's licence.

headlineQuote: A healthy bank balance doesn't turn my vocational certificate into an electrician's licence.
portrait: Bianca is a **58-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still learning practical tasks after the bookshop where she worked closed.
She has **seventeen months saved**, higher pay and many local firms; partner Robin handles archive records, and their children are grown.
She uses **AI daily**, but practical tasks remain within ability and a qualified supervisor's permission and checks, with no licence or sign-off.
Her **shared demonstration request** requires consent, no fees, protected weekly pay and hours and written agreement, without assuming income or jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected major loss of Robin's archive income before replacement, with later physical risk to her junior tasks.
whatWouldHelp: **Named paid demonstrations**, protected normal weekly wages and hours, and available advice on actual records would help.
